title: Digestive Tract Parts and Abdominal Regions
body:
## What it is
The GI tract is one long tube (roughly 23-26 feet) running from the mouth through the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus.

## Must-know facts
- **Esophagus:** about 25 cm long, sits in the mediastinum in front of the spine and behind the trachea; it only carries food from mouth to stomach.
- **Stomach:** a stretchy muscular pouch that holds about 1,500 mL and stores food while enzymes begin breaking it down.
- **Small intestine:** the longest segment and the place where nutrients are absorbed. Three parts in order: duodenum, jejunum, ileum.
- **Large intestine:** ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, then rectum. Waste arrives here and elimination begins.

## Physical examination
- Order of abdominal assessment: inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation. Palpation and percussion come after listening because touching can change bowel sounds.
- The handout lists palpation starting at the right lower quadrant, then right upper, left upper, left lower (a clockwise sweep).

## Abdominal regions and what lies under them
- **Right hypochondriac:** right liver lobe, gallbladder, part of duodenum, hepatic flexure, upper right kidney.
- **Epigastric:** aorta, pyloric end of stomach, pancreas, part of liver.
- **Left hypochondriac:** stomach, spleen, tail of pancreas, splenic flexure, upper left kidney.
- **Right lumbar:** ascending colon, lower right kidney. **Umbilical:** omentum, mesentery, lower duodenum, parts of jejunum and ileum.
- **Right inguinal:** cecum, appendix, end of ileum, right ureter, ovary or spermatic cord. **Left inguinal:** sigmoid colon, left ureter, ovary or spermatic cord.
- **Hypogastric:** ileum, plus bladder or uterus when enlarged.
- Use this map to reason about pain location: RUQ points to liver/gallbladder, RLQ to appendix.

## Related topics
[[Digestion, Absorption and Digestive Enzymes]], [[Appendicitis]], [[Cholelithiasis and Cholecystitis]]

## Check against your textbook
Most textbooks say to palpate lightly and start in the quadrant farthest from the painful area; the handout's fixed order is only one convention.

title: Digestion, Absorption and Digestive Enzymes
body:
## The three jobs
- **Digestion:** enzymes and secretions break proteins, fats and sugars into small molecules.
- **Absorption:** small molecules, vitamins and minerals pass through the intestinal wall into the blood.
- **Elimination:** waste is removed after digestion and absorption.

## Step by step
- **Mouth:** chewing and swallowing start digestion. About 1.5 L of saliva a day comes from the parotid, submaxillary and sublingual glands. Salivary amylase begins starch digestion. Swallowing starts voluntarily, then the swallowing center in the medulla takes over.
- **Stomach:** secretes strongly acidic fluid (hydrochloric acid). Chief cells make pepsinogen, which becomes pepsin, the key protein-digesting enzyme. The gastric lining also makes **intrinsic factor**, which binds dietary vitamin B12 so it can be absorbed. Food stays from 30 minutes to several hours depending on volume, osmotic pressure and chemical makeup.
- **Small intestine:** amylase (starch), lipase (fat), trypsin (protein). Bile is made by the liver, stored in the gallbladder and emulsifies fat so it can be digested and absorbed. Daily secretions: about 1 L pancreatic juice, 0.5 L bile, 3 L from small intestine glands. Segmentation contractions mix and churn; peristalsis pushes contents toward the colon.
- **Colon:** bacteria finish breaking down waste. Slow, weak peristalsis lets the colon reabsorb water and electrolytes, which is its main job. Strong intermittent waves move stool to the rectum in about 12 hours.

## Why it matters
- Loss of intrinsic factor (damaged stomach lining) leads to vitamin B12 deficiency, which is why gastritis lists B12 deficiency.
- Fat digestion needs bile plus pancreatic lipase, so gallbladder or pancreas disease causes fatty stools.

## Related topics
[[Gastritis]], [[Acute Pancreatitis]], [[Liver, Gallbladder and Pancreas Structure and Function]], [[Digestive Tract Parts and Abdominal Regions]]

title: Upper and Lower GI Series (Barium Studies)
body:
## What they are
- **Upper GI series (barium swallow):** contrast outlines the upper GI organs and sphincters. Detects ulcers, varices, tumors, regional enteritis, malabsorption and structural or functional problems.
- **Lower GI series (barium enema):** x-rays of the lower GI tract after barium is given by enema. Takes about 15-30 minutes.

## Priority nursing actions
- **Upper GI:** clear liquids then NPO from midnight. Advise against smoking, chewing gum and mints because they stimulate gastric motility and spoil the picture. Increase fluids afterwards so stool and barium are flushed out. Oral medicines are usually held that morning and resumed in the evening, but each client's regimen is reviewed individually.
- **Lower GI:** first ask about **allergy to iodine or contrast**. The bowel must be empty and clean: low-residue diet 1-2 days before, clear liquids, NPO after midnight, cleansing enemas until returns are clear. Laxative before and after.
- **After the test (both):** push fluids and check that the client passes the barium. Retained barium can harden and cause constipation or obstruction, so report white or absent stools.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Which instruction is correct before a barium enema?" Pick bowel cleansing, low residue diet, and allergy check.
- "Which finding after barium means follow-up?" No stool passed for days or abdominal distention.

## Related topics
[[Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) Nursing Care]], [[ERCP, Colonoscopy and Laparoscopy]]

## Check against your textbook
The advice that retained barium causes obstruction and that stool turns white is standard teaching I added; it is not in the handout.

title: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) Nursing Care
body:
## What it is
Direct look at the esophagus, stomach and duodenal lining through a lighted flexible scope. It takes about 30 minutes. The client may feel nausea, gagging or choking.

## Before the procedure
- NPO for 8 hours.
- Local anesthetic gargle or spray; moderate sedation (midazolam [Versed]) to relieve anxiety. Atropine may reduce secretions and glucagon may relax smooth muscle.
- Position **left lateral** so secretions drain from the mouth and the scope enters smoothly.
- A mouth guard stops the client biting the scope. Protect the scope: the fiberoptic bundles break if bent sharply.

## After the procedure (priority order)
1. **Airway first.** Topical anesthesia and sedation depress the gag reflex, so monitor and maintain the oral airway (Maslow: airway before comfort).
2. Check level of consciousness, vital signs, oxygen saturation and pain.
3. Watch for **perforation**: pain, bleeding, unusual difficulty swallowing, rapid rise in temperature.
4. Keep NPO until the gag reflex returns, then offer lozenges, saline gargle or oral analgesics for a sore throat.
5. Sedated clients stay in bed until fully alert.

## How the exam asks about it
A common question: "Which action first after EGD?" Check gag reflex and airway before offering food or fluids.

## Related topics
[[ERCP, Colonoscopy and Laparoscopy]], [[Barrett's Esophagus]], [[Peptic Ulcer Disease: Gastric versus Duodenal Ulcer]]

title: ERCP, Colonoscopy and Laparoscopy
body:
## ERCP
- An endoscope plus x-ray (contrast) to see the common bile duct, pancreatic duct and hepatic ducts, entering through the ampulla of Vater in the duodenum.
- Used for gallstones, bile duct blockage and pancreatic problems.

## Colonoscopy
- Direct look at the whole large intestine: anus, rectum, sigmoid, transverse, descending and ascending colon.
- Therapeutic use: visible polyps can be removed with a snare and cautery through the scope.

## Laparoscopy
- Direct view of organs inside the abdomen to find growths, abnormalities and inflammation; biopsies can be taken.
- Carbon dioxide is injected into the peritoneal cavity (**pneumoperitoneum**) to lift the intestines away from the pelvic organs.
- Usually done under general anesthesia; the stomach and bowel sometimes need decompressing first.

## Nursing points
- Clients need bowel preparation for colonoscopy and NPO status before ERCP and laparoscopy, as ordered.
- Monitor after any scope for perforation (pain, bleeding, fever) and recovery from sedation or anesthesia.
- After laparoscopy, shoulder pain is common because of leftover gas (textbook point, see below).

## Related topics
[[Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) Nursing Care]], [[Gallstone Treatment and Biliary Drainage Care]], [[Diverticulosis and Diverticulitis]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout gives few nursing details here. Bowel prep, post-procedure monitoring and shoulder pain after laparoscopy are standard teaching I added, so verify them.

title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
body:
## What it is
Backward flow of stomach and duodenal contents into the esophagus because the **lower esophageal sphincter (LES)** is weak or incompetent.

## Must-know facts
- Classic symptom: **pyrosis** (burning behind the breastbone). Others: dyspepsia, dysphagia, hypersalivation, esophagitis.
- Symptoms can mimic a heart attack. History helps tell them apart, but chest pain is still treated as cardiac until ruled out (Maslow: circulation/oxygenation first).
- Tests: endoscopy or barium swallow, 12-36 hour ambulatory esophageal pH monitoring, bilirubin monitoring (Bilitec).

## Treatment
- **Antacids** neutralize acid.
- **H2 receptor blockers** lower acid by blocking histamine at the parietal cells.
- **Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)** slow the acid pump of parietal cells; more potent than H2 blockers.
- **Prokinetic agents** increase propulsive movement of the gut.
- Surgery: **Nissen fundoplication**, wrapping the gastric fundus around the lower esophagus.

## Client teaching (the usual test question)
- Avoid what lowers LES pressure or irritates: caffeine, tobacco, beer, carbonated drinks, spicy and fatty foods.
- Low-fat diet, keep a normal weight, wear loose clothing.
- Do not eat or drink 2 hours before bed and do not lie down after meals.
- Raise the head of the bed 6-8 inches.

## Complications
Long-standing reflux can lead to [[Barrett's Esophagus]]. Related: [[Hiatal Hernia]], [[Peptic Ulcer Drugs and Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout says prokinetics enhance "colonic transit"; they actually speed gastric emptying and upper gut movement. It also lists milk as something to avoid; confirm with your textbook.

title: Barrett's Esophagus
body:
## What it is
A change in the lining of the lower esophagus caused by long-term acid reflux (GERD). The normal squamous cells are replaced by a different cell type (metaplasia). It is a **precursor to esophageal cancer**.

## Must-know facts
- Same symptoms as GERD: pyrosis, dyspepsia, dysphagia, hypersalivation, esophagitis.
- Diagnosis: EGD with **biopsy** (biopsy proves the cell change).

## Treatment
- Control reflux first (see [[Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)]]).
- Destroy abnormal cells: **photodynamic therapy** or **laser thermal ablation**.
- **Esophagectomy** for advanced disease: removal of the esophagus with a wide tumor-free margin and nearby lymph nodes.

## Nursing focus
- Teach that untreated reflux can become cancer, so follow-up endoscopy matters.
- Teach reflux control: small meals, head of bed raised, avoid late meals.

## How the exam asks about it
"Complication of long-term GERD that raises cancer risk?" Answer: Barrett's esophagus. "Test to confirm?" EGD with biopsy.

## Related topics
[[Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) Nursing Care]], [[Hiatal Hernia]]

title: Hiatal Hernia
body:
## What it is
The opening in the diaphragm where the esophagus passes becomes enlarged, so part of the upper stomach moves up into the chest.

## Types
- **Sliding:** upper stomach and the gastroesophageal junction slide up through the opening (the common type).
- **Paraesophageal (rolling):** all or part of the stomach pushes through the diaphragm beside the esophagus.

## Manifestations
Heartburn, regurgitation, dysphagia, fullness after eating, chest pain.

## Diagnosis
X-ray, barium swallow, fluoroscopy.

## Management
- Medicines as for GERD (antacids, H2 blockers, PPIs).
- Small frequent meals; do not recline for 1 hour after eating; raise the head of the bed.
- Surgery in about 15% of clients: **Nissen fundoplication**.

## Why the advice makes sense
Gravity helps keep stomach contents down, and a smaller stomach load means less pressure pushing through the opening.

## Related topics
[[Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)]], [[Barrett's Esophagus]]

title: Gastritis
body:
## What it is
Inflammation of the stomach lining.

## Causes
Repeated irritants (highly seasoned food), overuse of **aspirin and NSAIDs**, excess alcohol, bile reflux, radiation therapy, swallowing strong acid or alkali, and the bacterium ***Helicobacter pylori***.

## Manifestations
Abdominal discomfort, headache, lassitude, nausea and vomiting, hiccupping, heartburn after eating, belching, intolerance of spicy or fatty foods, and vitamin B12 deficiency (the damaged lining loses intrinsic factor).

## Assessment and diagnosis
- Low or absent stomach acid (hypochlorhydria, achlorhydria).
- Upper GI series or endoscopy; biopsy of tissue.

## Treatment
- H2 blockers, PPIs, and antibiotics (amoxicillin, clarithromycin) when H. pylori is present.
- Surgery rarely: gastrojejunostomy (joining jejunum to the stomach to bypass the pylorus).

## Priority nursing actions
- Remove the cause: no alcohol, spicy or fatty foods, aspirin or NSAIDs until symptoms settle; discourage caffeine.
- **Watch for hemorrhagic gastritis**: hematemesis, tachycardia, hypotension. Report at once (bleeding is a circulation emergency).

## Related topics
[[Peptic Ulcer Disease: Gastric versus Duodenal Ulcer]], [[Peptic Ulcer Drugs and Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome]], [[Digestion, Absorption and Digestive Enzymes]]

title: Peptic Ulcer Disease: Gastric versus Duodenal Ulcer
body:
## What it is
A sore (excavation) in the lining of the stomach, pylorus or duodenum. Main cause: H. pylori infection. Contributors: excess acid from caffeine, spicy food, smoking, alcohol, NSAIDs and stress.

## Duodenal versus gastric ulcer (the exam favorite)
- **Duodenal:** age 30-60; about 80% of peptic ulcers; acid **hypersecretion**; possible weight gain; pain 2-3 hours after meals and **relieved by eating**; vomiting uncommon; hemorrhage less likely; melena more common than hematemesis; malignancy rare.
- **Gastric:** usually age 50 and over; about 15% of peptic ulcers; normal or low acid; **weight loss**; pain 30-60 minutes after meals and **aggravated by eating**; vomiting common; hemorrhage more likely; hematemesis more common than melena; cancer possible occasionally.
- Risk factors listed: alcohol, smoking, stress, H. pylori (duodenal); H. pylori, gastritis, alcohol, NSAIDs, stress (gastric).

## Memory aid (made up)
Duodenal = "Dines, Dulls" (eating relieves it, pain returns hours later, client gains weight). Gastric = "Gets worse with Grub" (eating hurts, client loses weight).

## Nursing management
- Stress reduction and rest, stop smoking.
- Avoid foods and drinks that irritate: alcohol, coffee, milk, spicy foods, soft drinks, tea, NSAIDs, aspirin.
- Watch for bleeding (black tarry stools, vomiting blood) and perforation (sudden severe pain, rigid abdomen), which need emergency action.

## Related topics
[[Gastritis]], [[Peptic Ulcer Drugs and Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome]], [[Gastric Surgeries: Vagotomy, Pyloroplasty and Billroth]]

## Check against your textbook
Milk was once advised for ulcers but is now often discouraged because it stimulates acid; the handout lists it as an irritant.

title: Peptic Ulcer Drugs and Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome
body:
## Drug groups
- **H2 blockers** (ranitidine, cimetidine): reduce acid by blocking histamine.
- **Proton pump inhibitors** (omeprazole): strongest acid reduction.
- **Antibiotics** to clear H. pylori.
- **Antacids:** neutralize acid already made.
- **Cytoprotectants** (sucralfate, misoprostol): sucralfate becomes a thick, sticky layer in acid that coats the ulcer base and blocks digestion by pepsin.

## Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
Severe, recurring peptic ulcers plus extreme stomach acidity caused by **gastrin-secreting tumors** (benign or malignant).

## Nursing points
- Give sucralfate on an empty stomach and separate it from other drugs and antacids as ordered (standard teaching, not in the handout).
- Reinforce triggers to avoid: NSAIDs, alcohol, smoking.

## How the exam asks about it
"Which drug protects the ulcer surface?" Sucralfate. "Tumor causing extreme acid and ulcers?" Zollinger-Ellison.

## Related topics
[[Peptic Ulcer Disease: Gastric versus Duodenal Ulcer]], [[Gastric Surgeries: Vagotomy, Pyloroplasty and Billroth]], [[Gastritis]]

## Check against your textbook
Ranitidine has been withdrawn in many countries over a contaminant concern; check which H2 blockers your syllabus expects. Misoprostol is a prostaglandin analogue and is dangerous in pregnancy (my addition).

title: Gastric Surgeries: Vagotomy, Pyloroplasty and Billroth
body:
## When surgery is used
For ulcers that do not respond to drugs, bleed, perforate or block the outlet. The aim is to cut acid or remove the acid-making area.

## The operations
- **Vagotomy and pyloroplasty:** cut the vagus nerve branches that stimulate acid secretion, and widen the pylorus so the stomach empties well.
- **Billroth I (gastroduodenostomy):** remove the lower antrum (the area with gastrin-secreting cells) and a bit of duodenum; join the remaining stomach to the duodenum.
- **Billroth II (gastrojejunostomy):** remove the lower stomach and join it to the jejunum; the duodenal stump is closed (oversewn).
- **Gastrojejunostomy** alone bypasses the pylorus.

## Memory aid (common, not from handout)
Billroth I joins to the first part (duodenum); Billroth II joins to the second part further down (jejunum).

## Complications to expect
Rapid gastric emptying causes [[Dumping Syndrome]] after these operations. Also watch for bleeding and leaks.

## Nursing focus
- After surgery check vital signs, bleeding, and nasogastric tube drainage as ordered (my addition).
- Teach small frequent dry meals, as in dumping syndrome.

## Related topics
[[Peptic Ulcer Disease: Gastric versus Duodenal Ulcer]], [[Peptic Ulcer Drugs and Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome]]

## Check against your textbook
Postoperative gastric care (NG tube care, diet progression) is not in the handout; use your surgical nursing text.

title: Dumping Syndrome
body:
## What it is
A group of GI and circulatory symptoms after gastric surgery or vagotomy. Food leaves the stomach too fast (rapid gastric emptying), so it is poorly mixed with pancreatic and bile secretions.

## Manifestations (about 30 minutes after eating)
- Nausea, vomiting, abdominal fullness and cramping, diarrhea, borborygmi.
- Palpitations, tachycardia, sweating, weakness, dizziness.
- Steatorrhea (fat in stool).

## Priority nursing actions and teaching
- **Lie down after meals** (slows emptying and helps blood pressure).
- Avoid sugar, salt and milk; keep carbohydrates low and avoid concentrated sweets; fat is allowed as tolerated.
- Antispasmodic drugs may be ordered to slow emptying.
- **Do not drink fluids with meals.** Drink up to 1 hour before or 1 hour after. Meals should contain more dry foods than liquids.
- Small, frequent meals (standard advice).

## Why it works
Liquids and sugary food are the fastest to wash through the stomach and pull water into the bowel, causing cramps, diarrhea and a drop in circulating volume.

## How the exam asks about it
"Which statement shows the client understands?" Correct answer: "I will lie down after eating and drink fluids between meals."

## Related topics
[[Gastric Surgeries: Vagotomy, Pyloroplasty and Billroth]], [[Peptic Ulcer Disease: Gastric versus Duodenal Ulcer]]

## Check against your textbook
Late dumping (low blood sugar 1-3 hours after eating) is in most textbooks but not this handout.

title: Diverticulosis and Diverticulitis
body:
## What it is
A diverticulum is a small pouch of bowel lining pushed through a weak spot in the muscle layer. Most are in the **sigmoid colon**.
- **Diverticulosis:** many pouches, no inflammation or symptoms.
- **Diverticulitis:** pouches inflamed or infected, because food and bacteria are trapped.

## Manifestations
Irregular bowel with spells of diarrhea, nausea, anorexia, bloating, narrow stools, constipation (sometimes obstruction), and signs of infection (fever, raised WBC, left lower quadrant pain, my addition).

## Diagnosis
Colonoscopy, barium enema, abdominal x-rays, and **CT scan, the test of choice for diverticulitis** (can show abscesses).

## Treatment
- Antibiotics, analgesics and anticholinergics for spasm.
- The handout says meperidine for pain and says **morphine is contraindicated** because it raises pressure inside the colon.
- Avoid lifting, straining, coughing and bending (raise abdominal pressure).
- Diet: soft, **high fiber** for diverticulosis; **low fiber** during an acute diverticulitis flare until infection settles. Avoid gas-forming foods.
- Surgery: colon resection with primary anastomosis; temporary or permanent colostomy if inflammation is severe.

## Complications to monitor
Perforation, hemorrhage, fistula, abscess, peritonitis.

## Related topics
[[Peritonitis]], [[Appendicitis]], [[Inflammatory Bowel Disease Treatment and Ileostomy Surgeries]]

## Check against your textbook
Opioid choice varies between sources (the old meperidine-over-morphine rule is debated); use the teaching your school uses. Colonoscopy is usually avoided during acute inflammation (my addition).

title: Crohn's Disease
body:
## What it is
Long-term inflammation that goes through **all layers** of the bowel wall (transmural). It most often affects the ileum and colon but can occur anywhere from mouth to anus. It leads to thickening, scarring, narrowing, ulcers, **fistulas** and abscesses, giving a classic **cobblestone** look. Areas can be affected with normal bowel between them (skip lesions, my addition).

## Manifestations
- Fever and raised WBC.
- Cramping, colicky pain **after meals**.
- Semi-solid diarrhea, sometimes with mucus or pus.
- Abdominal distention, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, weight loss.
- Anemia, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance.

## Compare with ulcerative colitis (made-up contrast)
- Crohn's: whole thickness, patchy, pain after meals, weight loss, fistulas.
- UC: surface layers only, continuous from the rectum upward, bloody liquid stools. See [[Ulcerative Colitis]].

## Priority nursing actions
Relieve inflammation (drugs), correct fluid and electrolyte loss, support nutrition, and watch for perforation, peritonitis and bleeding. Details are in [[Inflammatory Bowel Disease Treatment and Ileostomy Surgeries]].

## Related topics
[[Ulcerative Colitis]], [[Diverticulosis and Diverticulitis]]

## Check against your textbook
Skip lesions and pain-after-meals mechanism are partly my additions. Diagnostic tests for Crohn's are not listed separately in the handout.

title: Ulcerative Colitis
body:
## What it is
Recurring ulceration and inflammation of the **mucosa and submucosa** of the colon and rectum.

## Risk factors in the handout
Higher prevalence in Caucasians and people of Jewish descent; NSAIDs make inflammatory bowel disease worse.

## Manifestations
- Anorexia, weight loss, malaise.
- **Diarrhea, 10-20 liquid stools a day.**
- Left lower quadrant tenderness and cramping.
- **Rectal bleeding.**
- Dehydration and electrolyte imbalance, anemia, hypocalcemia, vitamin K deficiency.

## Diagnosis
Colonoscopy, sigmoidoscopy, barium enema, CBC, abdominal x-ray, stool examination.

## Priority nursing actions
- Fluid and electrolyte replacement; NPO during an acute attack with IV fluids.
- Monitor stool count, weight, hemoglobin and signs of bleeding or perforation.
- See [[Inflammatory Bowel Disease Treatment and Ileostomy Surgeries]] for drugs, diet and operations.

## How the exam asks about it
A client with bloody diarrhea and left lower cramping: think UC. Which surgery cures it? Total removal of the colon.

## Related topics
[[Crohn's Disease]], [[Diverticulosis and Diverticulitis]]

## Check against your textbook
UC is limited to the colon and rectum (this handout agrees). Colonoscopy and barium enema are usually avoided in a severe flare (my addition).

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease Treatment and Ileostomy Surgeries
body:
## Drug therapy (priority: relieve inflammation)
- **Salicylate compounds:** for mild-moderate disease and to prevent relapse in maintenance.
- **Corticosteroids:** for severe, fulminant disease; oral for outpatients, IV in hospital.
- **Immunosuppressants:** alter the immune response (exact action in IBD unclear).
- **Anti-diarrheals:** reduce peristalsis to rest the bowel; continued until stools return near normal.

## Nursing care
- NPO and IV fluids and electrolytes in acute attacks; parenteral nutrition if ordered.
- Diet when eating: **low residue, high protein, high calorie**, vitamin supplements and iron.
- Avoid gas-forming foods.
- Monitor for perforation, peritonitis and hemorrhage.

## Surgery
- **Proctocolectomy with permanent ileostomy:** removal of colon and rectum; an ileal stoma on the abdominal wall.
- **Kock (continent) ileostomy:** a pouch made from distal ileum with a stoma that is emptied by catheter.
- **Restorative proctocolectomy:** the procedure of choice when the rectum can be spared; makes an ileal reservoir that acts as a "new" rectum, keeping sphincter control, with no permanent ileostomy.
- **Ileoanal anastomosis:** ileum pouch connected to the anus after removing the colon and rectal mucosa.

## Related topics
[[Crohn's Disease]], [[Ulcerative Colitis]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout is vague about names for pouch operations; "ileorectostomy" in textbooks usually means ileum joined to the rectum, not an ileoanal pouch. Verify.

title: Appendicitis
body:
## What it is
Inflammation of the appendix, a finger-like pouch about 10 cm long attached to the cecum below the ileocecal valve. Most common between ages 10 and 30. It is blocked or kinked by a **fecalith**, tumor or foreign body.

## Assessment findings
- Vague epigastric or periumbilical pain that moves to sharp, well-localized **right lower quadrant** pain.
- Low-grade fever, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite.
- **Rebound tenderness** (pain on release of pressure).
- **Rovsing's sign:** pressing the left lower quadrant causes pain in the right lower quadrant.
- Raised WBC; imaging by x-ray, ultrasound or CT (right lower quadrant density). Pregnancy test rules out ectopic pregnancy.

## Priority nursing actions
- Suspect appendicitis, keep NPO and report; do not give laxatives or apply heat (standard teaching, my addition) because they may cause rupture.
- IV fluids, antibiotics, analgesics as ordered.
- **Appendectomy** as soon as possible to prevent perforation. If abscess, place a drain.
- Watch for sudden relief of pain then fever and rigid abdomen: perforation.

## After surgery
- **High Fowler's position** to reduce tension on the incision and organs.
- Teach: sutures removed on day 5-7, incision care, avoid heavy lifting; normal activity within 2-4 weeks.

## Complications
Perforation, [[Peritonitis]], abscess, portal pylephlebitis (septic thrombosis of the portal vein).

## Related topics
[[Digestive Tract Parts and Abdominal Regions]], [[Diverticulosis and Diverticulitis]]

## Check against your textbook
McBurney's point and the no-laxative/no-heat rule are standard but not in the handout. Some books say semi-Fowler's after surgery.

title: Hemorrhoids
body:
## What it is
Swollen veins in the anal canal.
- **Internal:** above the internal sphincter; usually painless until they bleed or prolapse.
- **External:** outside the external sphincter; painful when thrombosed because of inflammation and edema.

## Causes
Age around 50, straining or shearing of the lining during defecation, and pressure from pregnancy.

## Manifestations
Itching, pain, **bright red bleeding**.

## Treatment
- Bulk-forming agents (psyllium), analgesic ointments and suppositories, astringents such as witch hazel.
- Procedures: infrared photocoagulation, bipolar diathermy, laser, sclerosing injections, rubber-band ligation, cryosurgery, hemorrhoidectomy.

## Nursing management and teaching
- Good personal hygiene.
- Avoid straining; **high-residue diet** with fruit and bran; more fluids.
- **Warm compresses and sitz baths**; bed rest during flare-ups.

## How the exam asks about it
"Best advice to prevent recurrence?" Fiber, fluids, no straining. Bright red blood on tissue points to rectal source, while black tarry stool suggests upper GI bleeding.

## Related topics
[[Portal Hypertension and Ascites]], [[Diverticulosis and Diverticulitis]]

title: Liver, Gallbladder and Pancreas Structure and Function
body:
## Liver
- Largest gland of the body, with four lobes: left, right, caudate, quadrate.
- Cell types include hepatocytes and Kupffer cells.
- Helps regulate blood glucose by making and storing glycogen in hepatocytes.
- Converts **ammonia** (from protein breakdown and gut bacteria) into **urea**. Failure of this job explains [[Hepatic Encephalopathy]].

## Gallbladder
Pear-shaped organ under the right lobe of the liver. Normally holds 30-50 mL of bile; up to 70 mL when fully distended. Bile emulsifies fats.

## Pancreas
Slender, fish-shaped organ lying behind the stomach, from the duodenum toward the spleen. It has both exocrine and endocrine roles. Pancreatic juice contains amylase, lipase and trypsin. The endocrine side (insulin, glucagon) is covered in [[Pancreatic, Kidney and Gonadal Hormones]].

## Why it matters
Liver, gallbladder and pancreas share the common bile duct opening (ampulla of Vater), so a stone or inflammation in one often involves another, for example gallstone pancreatitis.

## Related topics
[[Liver Cirrhosis]], [[Cholelithiasis and Cholecystitis]], [[Acute Pancreatitis]]

title: Viral Hepatitis A to E
body:
## What it is
Inflammation of liver tissue from viruses (A, B, C, D, E) or toxins and drugs. Damage comes from the immune response and causes local cell death.

## The three stages
- **Pre-icteric:** vague flu-like illness: malaise, fatigue, headache, muscle aches, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea.
- **Icteric** (days to weeks later): jaundice, dark urine, light-colored stool, steatorrhea, enlarged liver.
- **Post-icteric (convalescent):** lasts a few weeks; fatigue lessens and appetite returns.

## The five viruses (handout values)
- **A:** fecal-oral; incubation 15-50 days; usually mild with recovery.
- **B:** blood, perinatal, sexual; incubation 28-160 days; may be severe.
- **C:** blood transfusion, sexual; incubation 15-160 days; often becomes chronic, carrier state, liver cancer.
- **D:** same routes as B; incubation 21-140 days; like B but carrier state likelier (occurs only with B).
- **E:** fecal-oral; incubation 15-65 days; like A but very severe in pregnant women.

## Diagnosis and management
Liver function tests and serum and urine bilirubin are raised. Treatment is supportive: immunoglobulins, vaccines (A and B), antivirals, rest, good nutrition, and preventing spread.

## Priority nursing actions
Standard precautions; enteric (fecal) precautions for A and E; hand washing; blood and body fluid care for B, C, D. Encourage rest and small high-calorie meals.

## Related topics
[[Liver Cirrhosis]], [[Hepatic Encephalopathy]]

## Check against your textbook
Incubation periods differ between books (for example hepatitis B 45-160 days); use your course numbers. Vaccine mention and precautions are my additions.

title: Liver Cirrhosis
body:
## What it is
Chronic liver disease where liver cells are widely destroyed and replaced by scar tissue and irregular regrowth.

## Types
- **Laennec's (alcoholic):** alcohol plus long-term poor nutrition.
- **Biliary:** from bile duct disease blocking bile flow.
- **Post-hepatic (postnecrotic):** after hepatitis.

## Manifestations
Enlarged, firm liver, chronic dyspepsia, constipation or diarrhea, gradual weight loss, **ascites**, splenomegaly, spider angiomas, **caput medusae**, portal hypertension, mental deterioration.

## Diagnosis
Liver biopsy, liver scan, liver function tests (ALT, AST), serum proteins, prothrombin time.

## Priority nursing actions
- Safety first: confusion risk, so orient the client, limit visitors, raise side rails, assist walking.
- Reduce ascites with diuretics; protect fragile skin; reduce bleeding risk (antacid or H2 blocker prevents GI bleeding).
- No alcohol.
- Nutrition: vitamins and supplements; **high protein early** to help healing; **low protein late** when ammonia rises and encephalopathy threatens.

## Related topics
[[Portal Hypertension and Ascites]], [[Esophageal Varices and Balloon Tamponade]], [[Hepatic Encephalopathy]], [[Viral Hepatitis A to E]]

## Check against your textbook
Many textbooks no longer restrict protein long term in cirrhosis; follow your syllabus. Low albumin and prolonged PT explain edema and bleeding (my explanation).

title: Portal Hypertension and Ascites
body:
## What it is
High pressure in the portal vein because blood cannot flow freely through a diseased liver. The blocked flow backs up and causes:
- Varicose veins in the esophagus and rectum (hemorrhoidal).
- Fluid collecting in the abdomen (**ascites**).
- Enlarged spleen.

## Manifestations
Ascites, rapid weight gain, shortness of breath, fluid wave and liver dullness on percussion, dilated veins around the umbilicus (**caput medusae**), enlarged spleen, fluid and electrolyte imbalance.

## Priority nursing actions
- Bed rest; diuretics as ordered.
- **Measure abdominal girth and weigh daily** (same time, same scale) to follow fluid change.
- Reduce edema: elevate head of bed for breathing, restrict sodium (standard teaching).
- Assist with **paracentesis** (client empties bladder first, my addition).
- Monitor serum ammonia and electrolytes.

## Why shortness of breath?
Fluid pushes up on the diaphragm. Position to ease breathing, a Maslow (oxygenation) priority.

## Related topics
[[Liver Cirrhosis]], [[Esophageal Varices and Balloon Tamponade]], [[Hepatic Encephalopathy]]

title: Esophageal Varices and Balloon Tamponade
body:
## What it is
Swollen, twisted veins in the lower esophagus caused by portal hypertension. They can rupture and bleed massively. Alcohol history is common.

## Manifestations
**Hematemesis and melena**, signs of massive hemorrhage, plus signs of cirrhosis (hepatic encephalopathy, ascites, dilated abdominal veins).

## Diagnosis
Endoscopy; ALT, AST, bilirubin raised; portal pressure measurements.

## Priority nursing actions
1. **Airway, breathing, circulation:** bleeding is life-threatening. Monitor level of consciousness, vital signs, urine output, and give blood as ordered.
2. Check for other bleeding: bruises, nosebleeds, petechiae, bleeding gums.
3. **Sengstaken-Blakemore tube** (balloon tamponade): four openings for gastric aspiration, esophageal aspiration, gastric balloon inflation, esophageal balloon inflation.
   - Keep **scissors at the bedside** to cut the tube if the client has breathing difficulty (it can migrate up and block the airway).
   - ICU monitoring; prevent the client pulling on or displacing the tube.
4. **Vasopressin** is listed as initial drug therapy.
5. **Sclerotherapy:** afterwards watch for bleeding, esophageal perforation, aspiration pneumonia, stricture.
6. **Variceal band ligation:** elastic band placed on the varix through an endoscope; complications are ulceration, dysphagia, chest discomfort, strictures.

## Related topics
[[Portal Hypertension and Ascites]], [[Liver Cirrhosis]], [[Hepatic Encephalopathy]]

## Check against your textbook
Today octreotide is often used instead of vasopressin, and beta blockers prevent rebleeding (my addition). Check which your syllabus expects.

title: Hepatic Encephalopathy
body:
## What it is
A brain syndrome caused by liver failure. The failing liver cannot turn ammonia into urea, so ammonia reaches the brain and depresses the central nervous system.

## Triggers raising ammonia
GI bleeding, high-protein diet, bacterial growth in the gut, uremia (and severe liver damage itself).

## Manifestations
- Mental changes from slight confusion to coma.
- **Asterixis (liver flap):** with arms out and hands dorsiflexed, the hands drop and snap back.
- **Fetor hepaticus:** sweet, slightly fecal breath odor.
- Constructional apraxia: deteriorating handwriting, cannot copy a star.
- Raised ammonia and bilirubin, prolonged prothrombin time.

## Management
- **Lactulose:** keeps ammonia in the ionized state (ammonium) and lowers colon pH, causes bowel evacuation, and changes gut bacteria so less ammonia is made.
- **Neomycin:** reduces ammonia-producing bacteria in the colon.
- Check ammonia daily; monitor neurological status for impending coma.
- Reduce or stop dietary protein if coma is near.
- Use **conservative doses** of sedatives or analgesics; the damaged liver cannot clear drugs.

## Priority nursing actions
Safety and airway first in a drowsy client, then treat the ammonia source (bleeding, constipation, protein load).

## Related topics
[[Liver Cirrhosis]], [[Esophageal Varices and Balloon Tamponade]]

title: Cholelithiasis and Cholecystitis
body:
## Definitions
- **Cholelithiasis:** stones (calculi) in the gallbladder, caused by changes in bile makeup or bile stasis (infection, cirrhosis, pancreatitis).
- **Cholecystitis:** acute or chronic gallbladder inflammation, usually from a stone blocking the cystic duct; also from trauma, burns, surgery, gram-negative sepsis or too much opioid use.

## Risk factors
Obesity, women with multiple pregnancies, certain ethnic groups (Native American, Southwestern US Hispanic), frequent weight change or rapid weight loss, high-dose estrogen, ileal disease or resection, cystic fibrosis, diabetes.

## Manifestations
- Stones: episodic cramping pain in the **right upper quadrant** or epigastrium, sometimes to the back near the right shoulder blade; nausea, vomiting, fat intolerance, epigastric distress, fever, jaundice.
- Cholecystitis: biliary colic, RUQ tenderness and rigidity, **Murphy's sign** (pain and breath-holding when you press under the right rib margin as the client breathes in), fever, nausea, heartburn, flatulence, vitamin deficiency.

## Diagnosis
Abdominal x-ray; **ultrasound is the test of choice**; cholescintigraphy (IV radioactive agent); cholecystography (iodine contrast); ERCP.

## Related topics
[[Gallstone Treatment and Biliary Drainage Care]], [[Acute Pancreatitis]], [[ERCP, Colonoscopy and Laparoscopy]]

## Check against your textbook
Memory aid for risk (common, not from handout): fat, female, fertile, forty. Check the handout's wording on opioids as a cause of cholecystitis.

title: Gallstone Treatment and Biliary Drainage Care
body:
## Medical measures
- **Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA)** dissolves small radiolucent stones.
- Analgesics (morphine in the handout) and antacids.
- Diet: low-fat liquids, high in protein and carbohydrate.

## Stone fragmentation (non-surgical)
- **Intracorporeal lithotripsy:** laser pulses break stones in gallbladder or common bile duct.
- **Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy:** repeated shock waves from outside the body.

## Surgery
- **Laparoscopic cholecystectomy:** small punctures, one at the umbilicus.
- **Open cholecystectomy:** gallbladder removed after the cystic duct and artery are tied; a drain may be left near the gallbladder if bile leaks (removed after about 24 hours). **Bile duct injury is a serious complication.**
- **Choledochostomy:** incision in the common bile duct to remove stones.

## Biliary drainage tube care
- Bile that does not drain may back up into the liver and blood (obstruction).
- The tube or collection bag may be kept **above abdominal level** if ordered, to prevent bile loss.
- Every 24 hours measure the amount and record color and character of bile.
- After several days the tube may be clamped 1 hour before and after meals so bile reaches the duodenum.
- Tube is removed in about 7-14 days.
- Protect skin around the tube from irritation by bile.

## Related topics
[[Cholelithiasis and Cholecystitis]], [[Acute Pancreatitis]], [[ERCP, Colonoscopy and Laparoscopy]]

## Check against your textbook
Many textbooks place bile drainage bags at or below abdominal level; follow the surgeon's order. Morphine versus meperidine for biliary pain differs between sources.
outlineRefs: Maintaining skin integrity and Promoting Biliary Drainage

title: Acute Pancreatitis
body:
## What it is
The pancreas digests itself with its own enzymes, mainly **trypsin**. It ranges from mild, self-limited illness to fatal hemorrhagic pancreatitis. Causes: alcoholism, gallbladder disease (cholecystitis), surgery on or near the pancreas.

## Manifestations
- Abdominal tenderness with back pain.
- Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, steatorrhea.
- Fever, jaundice, mental confusion.
- Hypotension and signs of hypovolemia.
- Bleeding signs: **Cullen's sign** (bluish periumbilical discoloration) and **Turner's sign** (flank or back discoloration).

## Diagnosis
Elevated **amylase and lipase**, raised WBC, **hypocalcemia**.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Pain relief (the handout names morphine as the drug of choice).
2. **NPO** to rest the pancreas and stop enzyme release.
3. Maintain fluids and electrolytes (hypovolemia is a main danger; Maslow circulation).
4. Medicines: H2 blockers or PPIs to cut acid, which stimulates the pancreas.
5. Later: promote nutrition.
6. Watch calcium: hypocalcemia signs include tetany, Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs.

## Related topics
[[Chronic Pancreatitis]], [[Cholelithiasis and Cholecystitis]], [[Hypoparathyroidism and Post-Thyroidectomy Tetany]]

## Check against your textbook
Older textbooks prefer meperidine (morphine can cause spasm of the sphincter of Oddi); the handout says morphine. Know both and follow your syllabus. NG suction in severe cases is not in the handout.

title: Chronic Pancreatitis
body:
## What it is
Long-lasting inflammation that causes permanent damage to pancreas tissue, from repeated acute attacks. More than half of cases involve alcoholism: long-term alcohol makes pancreatic juice rich in protein, which plugs ducts and forms stones.

## Manifestations
- Recurring severe upper abdominal and back pain.
- Weight loss and anorexia.
- **Steatorrhea:** frequent, frothy, foul-smelling, fatty stools from poor fat digestion.

## Diagnosis
Raised lipase and amylase, raised WBC, ERCP to show pancreatic calcification, abnormal glucose tolerance test (insulin-making cells damaged).

## Management
- Pancreatic enzymes with meals, non-opioid pain relievers, antacids, H2 blockers, PPIs.
- Relieve pain, promote comfort, treat new attacks.
- **Avoid alcohol, caffeine** and foods that cause discomfort.
- Treat diabetes with diet and insulin or oral agents.
- Surgery: pancreatic jejunostomy (Roux-en-Y) to drain the duct, or a Whipple resection (pancreaticoduodenectomy) for pain.

## Related topics
[[Acute Pancreatitis]], [[Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnosis and Types]]

title: Peritonitis
body:
## What it is
Inflammation of the peritoneum, the membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering organs. Usually bacterial.

## Causes
Infection, trauma, spread from an outside organ, appendicitis, perforated ulcer, diverticulitis, bowel perforation, abdominal surgery, peritoneal dialysis.

## Manifestations
- Diffuse pain that becomes constant and localized, worst over the site of irritation.
- **Rigid, tender abdomen** and rebound tenderness.
- Paralytic ileus, anorexia, nausea, vomiting.
- Fever and rapid pulse.

## Diagnosis
Raised WBC; altered potassium, sodium and chloride; x-ray shows distended bowel loops.

## Priority nursing actions
- Treat the dehydration: fluid and colloid replacement.
- Analgesics, antiemetics, antibiotics, oxygen by nasal cannula or mask.
- **Intestinal intubation and suction** to relieve distention and restore bowel function.
- Position on the side with knees flexed to reduce abdominal tension.
- Protect drains from being pulled out.
- Surgery to remove or repair the cause (excision, resection, repair, drain abscess).

## Related topics
[[Appendicitis]], [[Diverticulosis and Diverticulitis]], [[Peptic Ulcer Disease: Gastric versus Duodenal Ulcer]]

title: Hypothalamus and Pituitary Hormones
body:
## Basics
- Glands release hormones straight into the blood; hormones act on target cells with matching receptors.
- Hormones regulate and integrate metabolism and work together with the nervous system.

## Hypothalamus
Makes releasing and inhibiting hormones that control the pituitary: CRH, TRH, GHRH, GnRH.

## Pituitary (hypophysis, the "master gland")
- **Anterior:** growth hormone (GH: bone and muscle growth, protein synthesis, fat use, less carbohydrate use); ACTH (stimulates adrenal cortex); TSH (thyroid); FSH (female: follicle growth and ovulation; male: sperm production); LH (female: corpus luteum, ovulation, estrogen and progesterone; male: testosterone); prolactin (prepares breasts for lactation); MSH.
- **Posterior:** **ADH (vasopressin)** makes the kidney reabsorb water; **oxytocin** contracts the pregnant uterus and ejects milk.

## Links to diseases
Too much GH: [[Gigantism]], [[Acromegaly]]. Too little: [[Pituitary Dwarfism and Hyperprolactinemia]]. ADH problems: [[SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH)]] (too much) and [[Diabetes Insipidus]] (too little).

## Check against your textbook
The handout labels "somatostatin" together with growth hormone; somatostatin is a separate hormone that inhibits GH and TSH release. Treat GH and somatostatin as different.

title: Adrenal, Thyroid and Parathyroid Hormones
body:
## Adrenal cortex (stimulated by ACTH)
- **Aldosterone** (mineralocorticoid): keeps sodium, loses potassium in the kidney.
- **Cortisol** (glucocorticoid): affects all nutrients, raises blood glucose, anti-inflammatory, helps with stress.
- Adrenal androgens: weak; turned into testosterone elsewhere.

## Adrenal medulla
Releases **epinephrine and norepinephrine** (sympathetic "fight or flight"): epinephrine turns liver glycogen into glucose and raises cardiac output; norepinephrine causes strong vasoconstriction.

## Thyroid (butterfly-shaped, lower neck)
- **T3 and T4** raise metabolic rate, protein and bone turnover. Most T3 comes from conversion of T4.
- **Calcitonin** lowers blood calcium and phosphate and blocks bone breakdown, released when calcium is high.

## Parathyroid (usually four, behind the thyroid)
**Parathormone (PTH)** raises blood calcium by drawing it from bone, kidney and intestines. They can be removed by accident in neck surgery, causing [[Hypoparathyroidism and Post-Thyroidectomy Tetany]].

## Quick opposites
Calcitonin down, PTH up for calcium. Insulin down, glucagon up for glucose.

## Related topics
[[Addison's Disease]], [[Cushing's Syndrome]], [[Hyperthyroidism and Graves' Disease]], [[Hyperparathyroidism]]

title: Pancreatic, Kidney and Gonadal Hormones
body:
## Pancreatic islets
- **Glucagon (alpha cells):** raises blood glucose by glycogenolysis (breaking down stored glucose) and gluconeogenesis (making new glucose from amino acids).
- **Insulin (beta cells):** lowers blood glucose by moving glucose into muscle, liver and fat cells.
- **Somatostatin (delta cells):** delays absorption of glucose from the gut.

## Kidney hormones
- **1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D:** increases calcium absorption from the intestine.
- **Renin:** starts the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
- **Erythropoietin:** increases red blood cell production.

## Gonads
- **Testes:** testosterone for male organs, secondary sex traits and sperm production.
- **Ovaries:** estrogen (female organs and traits) and progesterone (prepares the uterine lining, maintains pregnancy).

## Related topics
[[Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnosis and Types]], [[Insulin Types: Onset, Peak and Duration]], [[Hypothalamus and Pituitary Hormones]]

title: Gigantism
body:
## What it is
Too much growth hormone in **children**, before the growth plates close, so the person grows very tall (7-8 feet). Noticed around puberty. Head, hands and feet enlarge.

## Cause
Usually a pituitary tumor of GH-making cells, which can raise intracranial pressure.

## Manifestations
Very tall, weak and lethargic, severe headaches, visual disturbance, double vision, loss of color discrimination, bone decalcification.

## Diagnosis
CT, MRI, serum pituitary hormone levels.

## Treatment
- Bromocriptine (handout: dopamine antagonist) and octreotide (Sandostatin).
- Surgery: hypophysectomy; stereotactic radiation therapy.

## Nursing care
Record height and head circumference, perioperative and radiation care, and help the child interact normally with peers (body image).

## Related topics
[[Acromegaly]], [[Hypophysectomy Nursing Care]], [[Pituitary Dwarfism and Hyperprolactinemia]]

## Check against your textbook
Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist, and octreotide is a somatostatin analogue (it lowers GH); the handout states both differently.

title: Acromegaly
body:
## What it is
Too much growth hormone in **adults** (growth plates already closed). Bones thicken in width, soft tissues and organs enlarge, but height does not increase.

## Manifestations
Broad skull, protruding jaw (prognathism), larger hands and feet, thick heel pads, heavy lips, enlarged tongue, coarse features, enlarged heart, brain and organs.

## Diagnosis
CT, MRI, serum pituitary hormones.

## Treatment
Bromocriptine, octreotide, hypophysectomy, stereotactic radiation.

## Nursing management
Prepare for irradiation or surgery. After surgery monitor for hemorrhage, transient diabetes insipidus, **clear nasal drainage (rhinorrhea = possible cerebrospinal fluid leak)**, adrenal and thyroid insufficiency, meningitis (fever, stiff neck, headache), visual changes. Also watch for high blood sugar, heart and neurologic problems.

## Exam angle
Gigantism = child, tall. Acromegaly = adult, bone widening, no height gain.

## Related topics
[[Gigantism]], [[Hypophysectomy Nursing Care]], [[Diabetes Insipidus]]

title: Hypophysectomy Nursing Care
body:
## What it is
Partial or complete removal of the pituitary gland, via transfrontal, subcranial or oronasal transsphenoidal approach.

## Before surgery
Teach deep breathing (coughing and straining afterwards are restricted).

## After surgery (priority points)
- **Raise head of bed** (handout: at least 2 weeks) to reduce pressure on the sella turcica and encourage drainage.
- Avoid activities that raise intracranial pressure (straining, coughing, bending).
- **Watch nasal drainage:** post-nasal drip, and test for glucose; glucose-positive clear fluid suggests CSF leak, which risks meningitis.
- Monitor intake and output and daily weight (watch for diabetes insipidus).
- Blood glucose monitoring and insulin therapy if needed; ulcer medicine; check stools for blood.
- Warm saline mouth rinses (no vigorous toothbrushing, my addition).
- Lifelong hormone replacement is needed if the whole gland is removed (my addition).

## Related topics
[[Acromegaly]], [[Diabetes Insipidus]], [[Gigantism]]

## Check against your textbook
Ranking of precautions varies; confirm with neurosurgical nursing text.

title: Pituitary Dwarfism and Hyperprolactinemia
body:
## Dwarfism (GH deficiency)
- Limited growth from too little GH in childhood.
- Findings: overweight for height, underdeveloped jaw, abnormal teeth position, high voice, delayed puberty.
- Tests: x-ray, CT, MRI, blood tests.
- Treatment: growth hormone (somatrem, somatropin).
- Nursing: psychological support and acceptance of body image changes; help with walking; avoid high-impact activity.

## Hyperprolactinemia
Too much prolactin, often from a prolactin-secreting tumor.
- Female: amenorrhea, galactorrhea (milk from breasts).
- Male: gynecomastia, decreased sex drive, impotence.

## Related topics
[[Gigantism]], [[Hypothalamus and Pituitary Hormones]]

title: SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH)
body:
## What it is
Too much ADH even though the blood is too dilute. The kidneys hold water, urine cannot be diluted, and **dilutional hyponatremia** develops. Mnemonic (made up): SIADH = Salt Is Absent, water Held.

## Causes
Lung cancer (bronchogenic), severe pneumonia, pneumothorax, other malignancies, head injury, brain surgery or tumor, infection, some drugs.

## Findings
- Low serum osmolality (<280 mOsm/kg) and low sodium; **urine sodium and osmolality high**; ADH high.
- Decreased urine output, **weight gain**, headache, confusion, lethargy, seizures, coma in severe hyponatremia, delayed deep tendon reflexes.

## Priority nursing actions
- **Restrict fluids** as ordered.
- Monitor intake and output, daily weight, labs and neurological status; assess mental status regularly.
- Seizure safety if sodium is very low.
- Drugs: furosemide (Lasix) to remove water; demeclocycline makes the kidneys less sensitive to ADH.
- Treat the underlying cause; explain procedures to the client.

## Compare with DI
SIADH: too much ADH, concentrated urine, fluid overload, low sodium. [[Diabetes Insipidus]]: too little ADH, dilute urine, dehydration, high sodium.

## Related topics
[[Hypothalamus and Pituitary Hormones]]

## Check against your textbook
Severe hyponatremia is treated with hypertonic saline in hospital (my addition). Furosemide use is usually with sodium replacement.

title: Diabetes Insipidus
body:
## What it is
Deficiency of ADH (vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary. The kidneys cannot concentrate urine, so large volumes of dilute urine are lost.

## Causes
- **Central:** head trauma, brain tumor, pituitary surgery or radiation, CNS infections (meningitis, encephalitis, TB), metastatic tumors.
- **Nephrogenic:** kidneys do not respond to ADH (low potassium, high calcium, lithium, demeclocycline).

## Manifestations
Extreme thirst (2-20 L fluid a day), **dilute urine specific gravity 1.001-1.005**, polyuria and nocturia, dehydration, weight loss, tachycardia, hypotension, weakness.

## Diagnosis
High plasma osmolality and sodium. **Water deprivation test:** kidneys cannot concentrate urine. **Vasopressin test:** if urine concentrates after ADH, it is central; if not, it is nephrogenic.

## Priority nursing actions
- Replace fluids; let the client drink in response to thirst.
- Monitor intake and output, daily weight, specific gravity, vital signs.
- **Desmopressin (DDAVP)** intranasal (or IM) for central DI; thiazides, mild salt restriction and prostaglandin inhibitors for nephrogenic DI.
- Teach medication use, follow-up and wearing a medical ID.

## Related topics
[[SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH)]], [[Hypophysectomy Nursing Care]]

title: Goiter
body:
## What it is
Enlarged thyroid causing visible neck swelling.
- **Toxic goiter:** with hyperthyroidism. **Non-toxic goiter:** with normal thyroid function (euthyroid).

## Types
- **Endemic (iodine-deficient) simple/colloid goiter:** the most common type. Usually only swelling; large ones may press on the trachea. Treatment: iodine supplements, iodized salt, SSKI.
- **Nodular goiter:** areas of overgrowth that enlarge slowly and may press on structures in the chest; some are malignant or overactive.
- **Thyroid cancer:** risk rises after radiation of the neck or chest in infancy or childhood.

## Nursing points
Prevention teaching in the community is iodized salt. Watch for breathing or swallowing difficulty when the gland is large.

## Related topics
[[Hyperthyroidism and Graves' Disease]], [[Hypothyroidism and Myxedema]]

title: Hyperthyroidism and Graves' Disease
body:
## What it is
Too much thyroid hormone. The usual cause is Graves' disease, an autoimmune disorder where antibodies stimulate the thyroid (diffuse toxic goiter).

## Manifestations (everything speeds up)
- Nervousness, irritability, tremors, palpitations, tachycardia.
- Heat intolerance, sweating, warm moist flushed skin.
- Increased appetite with weight loss, diarrhea, amenorrhea.
- **Exophthalmos** (bulging eyes, startled look); von Graefe's sign (lid lag on looking down); Dalrymple's sign (upper lid retraction).
- Goiter, osteoporosis, enlarged heart muscle.

## Diagnosis
Thrill and bruit over the neck; **low TSH**, **high free T4**, **high radioactive iodine uptake**.

## Nursing management
- Nutrition: high calorie, high protein; avoid highly seasoned foods and stimulants; weigh and record intake.
- Coping: calm, unhurried approach; quiet, uncluttered environment.
- Temperature: keep the room cool; cool baths and fluids.
- Eye care: protective drops or ointment; discourage smoking.

## Related topics
[[Hyperthyroidism Treatment and Thyroidectomy Care]], [[Hypothyroidism and Myxedema]], [[Goiter]]

## Check against your textbook
Thyroid storm signs (high fever, severe tachycardia, agitation) are not described in the handout; know them as an emergency.

title: Hyperthyroidism Treatment and Thyroidectomy Care
body:
## Radioactive iodine
Destroys overactive thyroid cells. Teach about thyroid storm; propranolol can control symptoms. Not for pregnant or breastfeeding women.

## Antithyroid drugs
- **PTU and methimazole (Tapazole)** block thyroid hormone synthesis.
- **Agranulocytosis** is the most serious side effect: report sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers; stop the drug and have blood counts done.
- Handout: methimazole is treatment of choice in pregnancy.

## Iodine compounds (adjunct)
Potassium iodide, Lugol's solution, SSKI reduce hormone release and gland blood supply. Give in milk or juice, through a straw to protect teeth. Beta blockers (propranolol) control sympathetic symptoms.

## Subtotal thyroidectomy (about five-sixths removed)
- Before: PTU until hyperthyroid signs resolve; propranolol for heart rate; iodine to reduce bleeding; stop aspirin and other drugs that prolong clotting for several weeks.
- **Iodism (iodine toxicity)** needs immediate stopping: swollen mouth lining, excess saliva, runny nose (coryza), skin rash.
- After surgery: airway first (see [[Hypoparathyroidism and Post-Thyroidectomy Tetany]] for laryngospasm and low calcium). Support the neck, check for bleeding behind the neck and hoarseness (standard teaching).

## Related topics
[[Hyperthyroidism and Graves' Disease]], [[Hyperparathyroidism]]

## Check against your textbook
Most books prefer PTU in first trimester and methimazole later; the handout simply says methimazole. Radioactive iodine is also avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding, as stated.

title: Hypothyroidism and Myxedema
body:
## What it is
Too little thyroid hormone, commonly from autoimmune thyroiditis. **Myxedema** is the thick, mucus-like swelling of tissue seen in severe disease.

## Manifestations (everything slows down)
Hair loss, brittle nails, dry thick skin, hoarse voice, slow speech, bradycardia, low temperature, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, fatigue, masklike face, enlarged tongue, amenorrhea, loss of libido, deafness, numbness and tingling, personality and thinking changes.

## Myxedema coma
Depression, drowsiness, lethargy, low respiratory drive (narcosis), and coma. It is an emergency: airway and breathing first.

## Management
- **Levothyroxine** (Synthroid) lifelong.
- Monitor for angina, dysrhythmia, or MI as metabolism rises (cholesterol and coronary disease are common).
- Thyroid hormone can raise blood glucose and cause bone loss.
- **Sedatives, analgesics and anesthetics act longer**: use caution.

## Nursing care
- Fatigue: space activities, assist with self-care, gentle stimulation.
- Cold intolerance: extra blankets and clothing; avoid cold and drafts.
- Constipation: fluids, fiber, mobility; sparing use of laxatives.

## Compare
[[Hyperthyroidism and Graves' Disease]] is the opposite picture.

## Related topics
[[Goiter]]

title: Hyperparathyroidism
body:
## What it is
Too much parathormone, causing bone decalcification and calcium kidney stones. Calcium is high.

## Manifestations (memory aid: "stones, bones, groans, moans")
Renal stones, bone and skeletal pain, pathologic fractures, shorter stature; nausea, vomiting, constipation; apathy, fatigue, muscle weakness; hypertension and dysrhythmias.

## Diagnosis
High calcium and parathormone, bone x-ray changes, ultrasound, MRI, thallium scan, fine-needle biopsy.

## Complication
**Hypercalcemic crisis**: neurologic, cardiovascular and renal symptoms; life-threatening.

## Treatment
Antacids, stool softeners, phosphate therapy, calcitonin, bisphosphonates, cytotoxic agents. **Parathyroidectomy** (criteria in the handout include age under 50, poor follow-up, very high calcium, high urine calcium, and 30% fall in renal function).

## Nursing management
- Fluids 2000 mL or more a day (cranberry juice listed); **avoid thiazide diuretics**.
- Walk and keep moving; do not restrict or add calcium.
- Before surgery: force fluids, strain urine for stones.
- After surgery: check for renal stones, hematuria or flank pain, assist ADL, encourage weight bearing, relieve constipation, and watch for hypocalcemia ([[Hypoparathyroidism and Post-Thyroidectomy Tetany]]).

## Related topics
[[Adrenal, Thyroid and Parathyroid Hormones]]

## Check against your textbook
Thiazides raise calcium so are avoided; the handout's surgery numbers are written unclearly (1.0 mg/dL above normal, urine calcium over 400 mg/day).

title: Hypoparathyroidism and Post-Thyroidectomy Tetany
body:
## What it is
Too little parathormone, usually after surgery that removes or damages parathyroid tissue (thyroidectomy, radical neck dissection). Result: **low calcium, high phosphate**.

## Manifestations
Tetany, numbness, tingling and cramps, stiff hands and feet, **bronchospasm and laryngospasm**, carpopedal spasm (**positive Trousseau's sign**), **positive Chvostek's sign**, dysphagia, photophobia, dysrhythmia, seizures, anxiety and irritability.

## Diagnosis
Serum calcium very low (5-6 mg/dL or lower per handout), high phosphate, x-ray calcification.

## Priority nursing actions (airway first)
1. **Keep calcium gluconate IV at the bedside**; give for tetany.
2. Watch for laryngeal spasm and keep a **tracheostomy set** available.
3. Seizure precautions; low-stimulus room (no noise, drafts, bright lights).
4. Long term: oral calcium salts, vitamin D (improves calcium absorption), parenteral parathormone (watch allergy), aluminum hydroxide after meals to bind phosphate.
5. Diet high in calcium, low in phosphorus; avoid milk, milk products and egg yolks (high phosphorus).

## Related topics
[[Hyperthyroidism Treatment and Thyroidectomy Care]], [[Hyperparathyroidism]], [[Acute Pancreatitis]]

title: Pheochromocytoma
body:
## What it is
Usually benign tumor of the adrenal medulla (chromaffin cells) that releases too much epinephrine and norepinephrine. It is a cause of hypertension curable by surgery, but fatal if missed.

## Manifestations
Vertigo, blurred vision, sweating, air hunger, palpitations, tachycardia, tremor, flushing, anxiety, nausea, vomiting. **Five H's:** hypertension, hyperhidrosis, hypermetabolism, hyperglycemia, headache.

## Diagnosis
- **24-hour urine VMA** (coffee, tea, bananas, chocolate, vanilla, aspirin may distort results).
- Plasma catecholamines drawn after 30 minutes of supine rest.
- Clonidine suppression test if unclear; CT, MRI, ultrasound.

## Treatment
Alpha blockers (phentolamine, phenoxybenzamine), nitroprusside, calcium channel blockers (nifedipine), beta blockers (propranolol). Surgery: **adrenalectomy**.

## Nursing management
- Bed rest with head of bed raised (reduces blood pressure).
- Monitor ECG, arterial pressure, fluids, electrolytes, glucose.
- Surgery: hydrate before, during and after; after, hypotension and hypoglycemia occur as catecholamines suddenly fall. Bilateral removal needs lifelong steroid replacement; teach never to skip doses.

## Related topics
[[Adrenal, Thyroid and Parathyroid Hormones]], [[Cushing's Syndrome]]

## Check against your textbook
Beta blockers should only be started after alpha blockade (otherwise blood pressure can rise); the handout does not say this. Palpating the abdomen can trigger a crisis (my addition).

title: Addison's Disease
body:
## What it is
Adrenal cortex insufficiency: not enough cortisol (and aldosterone). Usually autoimmune or idiopathic atrophy. Pituitary ACTH is high.

## Manifestations
Muscle weakness, anorexia, fatigue, weight loss, **dark pigmentation**, hypotension, **low glucose, low sodium, high potassium**, leukocytosis.

## Addisonian crisis
Circulatory shock: cyanosis, pallor, anxiety, rapid weak pulse, rapid breathing, low BP. Precipitated by stress or infection.

## Diagnosis
Low early-morning cortisol, high ACTH, low glucose, low sodium, high potassium.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Crisis: **IV hydrocortisone**, then dextrose 5% in normal saline; vasopressors if hypotension continues; antibiotics if infection.
2. Increase glucocorticoid during stress or illness.
3. Teach: eat sodium-rich foods during GI illness or hot weather, take replacement exactly as prescribed, adjust dose in illness, avoid stress, **inform dentists and other providers**, wear medical alert bracelet.

## Compare
[[Cushing's Syndrome]] is the opposite (too much cortisol).

## Related topics
[[Adrenal, Thyroid and Parathyroid Hormones]]

title: Cushing's Syndrome
body:
## What it is
Too much cortisol. Most often from long-term corticosteroid drugs; less often from adrenal hyperplasia or a pituitary tumor.

## Manifestations
Buffalo hump, **central obesity with thin limbs**, moon face, thin fragile skin, bruising, slow healing, acne, weakness, hypertension, weight gain, hirsutism and virilization, breast atrophy, loss of libido.

## Labs
Dexamethasone suppression test (cortisol not suppressed in true disease, my addition). Findings: high sodium, high glucose, **low potassium**, fewer eosinophils, shrunken lymphoid tissue, raised plasma and urinary cortisol.

## Treatment
- Adrenal enzyme inhibitors: metyrapone, aminoglutethimide, mitotane, ketoconazole.
- Surgery: transsphenoidal hypophysectomy or bilateral adrenalectomy (lifelong replacement), pituitary radiation. Hydrocortisone after adrenalectomy.

## Nursing management
- Protective environment (infection risk, fragile skin); meticulous skin care.
- Rest periods through the day.
- Diet: high protein, calcium, vitamin D; **low carbohydrate, low sodium**.
- Monitor glucose, BP, fluid retention.

## Related topics
[[Addison's Disease]], [[Hypophysectomy Nursing Care]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's heading and description mix Cushing's disease (pituitary) with Cushing's syndrome (any cause); the dexamethasone test explanation is garbled.

title: Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnosis and Types
body:
## What it is
A group of metabolic diseases with high blood glucose from faulty insulin secretion, insulin action, or both.

## Risk factors
Family history, obesity, certain ethnic groups, age over 45, hypertension, low HDL (<35) and high triglycerides (>250).

## Classification
Type 1, type 2, gestational diabetes, and diabetes from other conditions.

## Diagnostic criteria (any one)
- Symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) plus **random glucose 200 mg/dL or more**.
- **Fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or more** (no calories for at least 8 hours).
- 2-hour glucose 200 mg/dL or more in an OGTT using a 75 g load.

## Type 1
Immune destruction of beta cells, so insulin is absent. Result: fasting high glucose, glucose cannot be stored after meals, **glycosuria** when glucose exceeds renal threshold (about 180-200 mg/dL), **osmotic diuresis** (loss of fluid and electrolytes), fat breakdown with **ketone bodies**, acidosis: [[Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)]]. Needs lifelong insulin.

## Type 2
Insulin resistance plus impaired insulin secretion, often with metabolic syndrome (hypertension, high cholesterol, abdominal obesity). Enough insulin remains to block ketone formation, so [[Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar Nonketotic Syndrome (HHNS)]] is the typical emergency.

## Related topics
[[Type 2 Diabetes Diet, Exercise and Monitoring]], [[Insulin Types: Onset, Peak and Duration]]

title: Type 2 Diabetes Diet, Exercise and Monitoring
body:
## Nutrition
- Weight loss of 1-2 pounds a week: subtract 500-1000 calories a day.
- Carbohydrates higher than fat or protein; sugars allowed in moderation (they are usually high in fat and low in nutrients).
- Dietary cholesterol under 300 mg/day.
- More fiber may improve glucose, reduce insulin need and lower cholesterol and LDL.
- Alcohol is absorbed first and needs no insulin; read labels of "health food" snacks for hidden carbohydrate and saturated fat.

## Exercise
- Lowers glucose by increasing muscle uptake and improving insulin use.
- Same time, same amount daily; walking is safe.
- **Eat a 15 g carbohydrate snack before moderate exercise** to avoid hypoglycemia.
- Proper footwear, inspect feet after exercise, avoid extreme heat or cold and avoid exercise when control is poor.

## Monitoring
- **Self-monitoring of blood glucose** prevents and detects both highs and lows.
- **HbA1c** shows average glucose over about 2-3 months.
- **Urine ketones** signal insulin deficiency: control of type 1 is worsening and DKA risk is high.

## Related topics
[[Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnosis and Types]], [[Oral Antidiabetic Drugs]], [[Hypoglycemia in Diabetes]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout says large amounts of alcohol raise DKA risk; most textbooks stress alcohol causing hypoglycemia. Verify.

title: Insulin Types: Onset, Peak and Duration
body:
## Why insulin
In type 1 diabetes, insulin must be given for life.

## Types (handout values)
- **Rapid-acting:** lispro (Humalog) onset 10-15 min, peak 1 h, duration 2-4 h; aspart (Novolog) 5-15 min, peak 40-50 min, 2-4 h; glulisine (Apidra) 5-15 min, peak 30-60 min, 2 h. For fast glucose lowering, mealtime highs, and nocturnal hypoglycemia prevention.
- **Short-acting (regular):** onset 0.5-1 h, peak 2-3 h, duration 4-6 h. Give 20-30 minutes before meals. **Clear. The only insulin for IV use.**
- **Intermediate (NPH, lente):** onset 2-4 h, peak 4-12 h, duration 16-20 h. Cloudy.
- **Long-acting (glargine [Lantus], detemir [Levemir]):** onset about 1 h, **no peak**, 24 h. Basal dose, once daily.

## Hypoglycemia timing
Hypoglycemia is most likely at each insulin's **peak**.

## Mixing rule
Regular is drawn up first when mixed with NPH ("clear before cloudy").

## Related topics
[[Insulin Storage, Mixing and Injection Technique]], [[Insulin Therapy Complications]], [[Hypoglycemia in Diabetes]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout contains typos ("Determir", product names). Do not mix glargine with other insulins (my addition). Human insulin acts faster/shorter than animal insulin reasoning in handout is unusual; verify.

title: Insulin Storage, Mixing and Injection Technique
body:
## Storage
- Unopened and spare vials in the refrigerator; never freeze; keep out of sunlight.
- The vial in use may stay at room temperature to reduce injection-site irritation.
- Always keep a spare vial.
- Gently roll or invert cloudy insulin; do not shake. Discard if a frosted whitish coating (flocculation) appears.

## Mixing and withdrawing
- Inject air into the vial equal to the dose, then withdraw.
- When mixing, **regular insulin is drawn first**, longer-acting insulin must be well mixed first.

## Injection sites
- Four areas: abdomen, back of upper arms, front of thighs, hips.
- Absorption is fastest in the **abdomen**, then arm, thigh, hip.
- Rotate within one area; keep each injection 0.5-1 inch from the last; avoid reusing a site within 2-3 weeks.
- **Do not inject into a limb about to be exercised**; absorption speeds up and may cause hypoglycemia.

## Technique
- Let alcohol dry first (wet alcohol burns and irritates).
- 90-degree angle for normal or overweight clients; aspiration generally not recommended in self-injection.
- Dispose of sharps in a puncture-resistant container.

## Related topics
[[Insulin Types: Onset, Peak and Duration]], [[Insulin Therapy Complications]]
outlineRefs: Selecting and Rotating the Injection Site

title: Insulin Therapy Complications
body:
## Reactions
- **Local allergic reaction:** redness, swelling, tenderness or a hard 2-4 cm wheal 1-2 hours after injection.
- **Systemic allergic reaction:** local reaction spreads to generalized hives, may include edema or anaphylaxis (rare, emergency).
- **Lipodystrophy:** local fat changes at injection sites: lipoatrophy (fat loss, dimpling or pitting) or lipohypertrophy (fat build-up). Prevent by rotating sites.
- **Insulin resistance:** common, most often from obesity; weight loss helps.
- **Morning hyperglycemia:** high glucose on waking; see [[Morning Hyperglycemia: Dawn Phenomenon, Somogyi Effect and Insulin Waning]].
- Any insulin excess causes [[Hypoglycemia in Diabetes]].

## Nursing points
- Absorption into lipodystrophic tissue is erratic, so avoid injecting there.
- Systemic reactions need immediate reporting.

## Related topics
[[Insulin Storage, Mixing and Injection Technique]]

title: Morning Hyperglycemia: Dawn Phenomenon, Somogyi Effect and Insulin Waning
body:
## Three causes of a high morning glucose
- **Insulin waning:** glucose rises steadily from bedtime to morning. Fix: raise the evening intermediate/long-acting dose, or add a pre-dinner dose.
- **Dawn phenomenon:** glucose is fairly normal until about 3 AM, then rises. Fix: move evening intermediate insulin from dinner to bedtime.
- **Somogyi effect:** normal or high at bedtime, **drops to low at 2-3 AM**, then rebounds through counter-regulatory hormones. Fix: **decrease** evening intermediate insulin or increase bedtime snack.

## How to tell them apart
Check glucose at about 3 AM. Low = Somogyi. Normal then rising = dawn phenomenon. High all night = waning.

## Key point
In Somogyi do not increase insulin; that worsens the swings.

## Related topics
[[Insulin Therapy Complications]], [[Hypoglycemia in Diabetes]]

title: Oral Antidiabetic Drugs
body:
## Drug groups
- **Sulfonylureas:** stimulate beta cells to release insulin and may improve insulin receptor binding. Hypoglycemia risk.
- **Biguanide (metformin):** lowers glucose made by the liver, improves tissue sensitivity to insulin, and lowers cholesterol synthesis. It is the only biguanide.
- **Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors:** slow absorption of complex carbohydrates in the intestine.
- **Meglitinides and phenylalanine derivatives (non-sulfonylurea secretagogues):** stimulate insulin release.
- **Thiazolidinediones (glitazones):** make tissues more sensitive to insulin.
- **DPP-4 inhibitors:** prolong incretin action, which raises insulin release and lowers glucagon.

## Nursing points
- Teach hypoglycemia signs for insulin-releasing drugs.
- Give with meals as ordered; oral agents do not replace diet and exercise.
- Metformin cautions (kidney function, contrast dye) are standard teaching I added.

## Related topics
[[Type 2 Diabetes Diet, Exercise and Monitoring]], [[Hypoglycemia in Diabetes]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout spells "dipeptide-pepidase" incorrectly; it is dipeptidyl peptidase-4. Specific drug names and timing (e.g. alpha-glucosidase inhibitors taken with the first bite of meal) are not given.

title: Hypoglycemia in Diabetes
body:
## What it is
Low blood glucose (handout: below 50-60 mg/dL) caused by too much insulin or oral drug, too little food, or extra exercise.

## Signs by severity
- **Mild:** sweating, tremor, tachycardia, palpitations, nervousness, hunger.
- **Moderate:** poor concentration, headache, confusion, memory lapses, numb lips and tongue, slurred speech, poor coordination, mood change or combative behavior, double vision, drowsiness.
- **Severe:** needs help from another person; disorientation, seizures, hard to wake, unconsciousness.

## Priority actions
1. If awake and able to swallow: give fast-acting sugar (about 15 g), then a snack.
2. If unconscious or cannot swallow: **glucagon 1 mg SC or IM**; in hospital 25-50 mL of **50% dextrose IV** (check the IV line is patent, it irritates veins).
3. Recheck blood glucose; follow with food when awake.

## Teaching
Eat extra when active, test glucose routinely, wear diabetic ID, always carry a simple sugar, avoid high-calorie, high-fat desserts to treat lows (they absorb slowly).

## How the exam asks about it
Sweating and shakiness on insulin: treat first, then investigate. Do not wait for a lab value when the client is symptomatic.

## Related topics
[[Insulin Types: Onset, Peak and Duration]], [[Morning Hyperglycemia: Dawn Phenomenon, Somogyi Effect and Insulin Waning]], [[Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)]]

## Check against your textbook
Most books define hypoglycemia as below 70 mg/dL. The 15 g carbohydrate treatment amount is standard but not in the handout.

title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
body:
## What it is
Caused by absent or very low insulin. Three features: **hyperglycemia, dehydration with electrolyte loss, and acidosis** from ketones.

## Manifestations
Polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, weakness, headache, orthostatic hypotension, weak rapid pulse, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, **acetone (fruity) breath**, **Kussmaul respirations** (deep, rapid).

## Findings
Glucose 300-800 mg/dL, bicarbonate 0-15 mEq/L, pH 6.8-7.3, low PCO2 (10-30 mm Hg), raised creatinine, BUN and hematocrit.

## Management (priority order)
1. **Rehydrate:** 0.9% saline (handout says 0.65 to 1 per hour for 2-3 hours); 0.45% saline if sodium is high; plasma expanders in severe hypotension. Watch for fluid overload: vital signs, lung sounds, intake and output.
2. **Potassium:** monitor often; serum K can fall fast as fluids and insulin work; start replacement once levels drop to normal (up to 40 mEq/h may be needed); ECG every 2-4 hours at first.
3. **Insulin:** slow continuous IV infusion. Flush the tubing and discard the first 50 mL because insulin sticks to the tubing.
4. **Avoid bicarbonate** in DKA: it causes further sudden drops in potassium.

## Related topics
[[DKA versus HHNS Comparison]], [[Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnosis and Types]], [[Hypoglycemia in Diabetes]]

## Check against your textbook
"0.65 to 1 Uh" in the handout looks like a typo (likely L/hour); verify. The sequence (fluids before insulin) is standard teaching.

title: Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar Nonketotic Syndrome (HHNS)
body:
## What it is
Very high glucose and osmolality with altered consciousness, but **little or no ketosis**. Persistent hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis and large water and electrolyte loss.

## Manifestations
Hypotension, profound dehydration (dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor), tachycardia, altered sensorium, seizures, hemiparesis.

## Findings
Glucose **600-1200 mg/dL**; osmolality above 350 mOsm/kg.

## Management
Fluids (0.9% or 0.45% saline), correct electrolytes (potassium added), insulin, central venous or hemodynamic monitoring. Insulin matters less than in DKA because acidosis does not need reversing.

## Priority
Rehydrate first; monitor neurological status and cardiovascular status.

## Related topics
[[DKA versus HHNS Comparison]], [[Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)]], [[Diabetes Mellitus: Diagnosis and Types]]

title: DKA versus HHNS Comparison
body:
## Side by side
- **Who:** DKA is mainly type 1 (can occur in type 2). HHNS is mainly older type 2.
- **Trigger:** DKA: missed insulin, stress (infection, surgery, stroke, MI). HHNS: physiologic stress.
- **Onset:** DKA rapid (under 24 h). HHNS slower, over days.
- **Glucose:** DKA usually above 250. HHNS usually above 600 mg/dL.
- **pH:** DKA low (about 7.3 or less). HHNS normal.
- **Ketones (blood and urine):** DKA present. HHNS absent.
- **Osmolality:** DKA 300-350. HHNS above 350.
- **Bicarbonate:** DKA below 15. HHNS normal.
- **BUN and creatinine:** elevated in both.
- **Mortality:** DKA under 5%. HHNS 10-40%.

## Memory aid (made up)
DKA = "Keto Acid" (ketones, acid, Kussmaul). HHNS = "Hyper-Hydration-Needed Severely".

## Related topics
[[Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)]], [[Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar Nonketotic Syndrome (HHNS)]]
